claims.statement: Paid subscriptions launched in 2019 at $64 MRR, with some of the 60 active beta users becoming paying subscribers.
Plausible reached 100 paying subscribers in 364 days and then grew to 427 paying subscribers and $2,750 MRR by July 2020.
Early growth came through Hacker News, Twitter, Google, Indie Hackers, GitHub, Reddit and content/community sharing without paid ads, affiliate marketing or sponsorships.
Plausible currently describes itself as self-funded and profitable, with subscription revenue funding team, infrastructure and product development.
Plausible positions against Google Analytics complexity, page weight, cookies/consent burden and closed-source opacity; the product is marketed as a lightweight privacy-friendly alternative.
The team reports that MIT licensing enabled proprietary competitors and cloud resellers, which motivated the switch to AGPLv3.
The founder reports roughly 30 paying customers after the first Hacker News launch, following a Product Hunt third-place result.
The first Hacker News position lasted about nine hours and produced roughly 30,000 page views; the founder then targeted developers because they could influence company analytics purchases.
At retrieval the open dashboard displayed approximately $50.7k MRR, 1,314 paying customers and approximately $609.4k ARR, while its detailed profit chart was stale by roughly 891 days.
Simple Analytics started paid-only, later introduced a free plan and then explored a reverse trial because the free plan slowed growth relative to the previous 4–5% MoM pace.
The current affiliate documentation offers 50% of the first year revenue, illustrated as $294 on a $588 annual business plan, while the founder says affiliates were not a major growth driver.
Simple Analytics targets Google Analytics privacy, cookie/banner, data-ownership, page-weight and GA4 migration friction; it frames the free incumbent as the central pricing blocker.
Cards Against Humanity bought the first paid plan after the initial version was built in about six weeks.
The early-access cohort reached about 56 customers with 39 converted to paid plans; the first public month later had 46 paying customers and about $1,400 monthly revenue.
Justin Jackson says his podcast, newsletter, Twitter and bootstrapper audience supplied roughly the first hundred customers, with personal networks producing further referrals.
Transistor used Reward Full and an ongoing 25% revenue affiliate program; affiliate-oriented podcast appearances and review sites became a distribution flywheel.
Transistor describes itself as bootstrapped and consistently profitable, with six people and more than 30,000 podcasts, while declining some complex enterprise deals.
Spotify and Apple link to Transistor-hosted feeds and audio; after a subscription ends, feeds are disabled and content is queued for deletion, with a migration/export window before billing ends.
Nomad List grew from a public city spreadsheet with roughly 75 cities and hundreds to about a thousand crowd contributors, followed by a number-one Hacker News launch.
The founder describes free city data alongside a paid social/community layer, with roughly 7,000 people paying for the community in the presentation.
Nomad List was reported at $30,416 monthly revenue on 2018-02-26 and at a $15k–$25k monthly membership range in another founder presentation.
The founder reports a day-one WordPress/Automattic sponsorship that paid a few thousand dollars per month and helped keep the site running during the first months.
The founder describes a single Linode VPS, two part-time contractors for security and moderation, no paid marketing and a mostly solo operation.
A domain/DNS incident took the site offline for about two days and was described as causing lost signups, revenue and profit.
Liinks emerged from Charlie Clark’s outreach to artists for the earlier VSUAL marketplace and was shipped about two weeks after development began.
The founder reported $25k MRR around August 2024 after roughly 4.5 years and describes Liinks as a solo bootstrapped business above $30k MRR on his profile.
Liinks initially priced Premium at $3, tested $2.99/$3.99/$5 and settled at $4 because higher prices reduced conversions; the current page shows $5 Starter and $12+ Pro.
Early growth used Instagram cold outreach and manually built pages, followed by product-led organic traffic from liinks.co URLs and a “Made with Liinks” badge.
Instagram ads worked before iOS14 but later stopped being cost effective; Google Ads were later reported at about $1/click and $30/conversion with Stripe-estimated LTV around $100.
The free tier was removed after low-quality and unwanted public-profile activity created manual review burden; active users fell but new paid users increased.

Across this five-case sample, early payment validation appears before fully mature product scope: Plausible started with a small dashboard, Simple Analytics with a minimal view, Transistor with a six-week version, Nomad List with an HTML table, and Liinks with a two-week launch.

The cases repeatedly convert borrowed distribution into owned recurring revenue: community launch surfaces, public data, creator badges, podcasts/newsletters, and developer recommendations are the acquisition layer while payment is captured in the product.

Public revenue signals are more available than owner take-home: all five cases expose some MRR/revenue/pricing, while payroll, tax, refunds, annual-prepay mix and founder draw remain incomplete, so waterfall estimates must remain scenarios.

observations.text: First traction was not a paid acquisition funnel: paid subscriptions began with beta users, then content and community posts reached Hacker News, Twitter, Google, Indie Hackers, GitHub, Reddit and other technical communities. The 100-paying-subscriber milestone took 364 days.

The incumbent weakness was not a shutdown but a visible product/policy gap: Google Analytics was presented as complex, heavy, privacy-invasive and opaque. Plausible used that friction as the wedge and later benefited from Google Analytics migration/regulatory discomfort.

The wallet trigger is the avoided cost of cookies, consent banners, privacy compliance work, page weight and confusing reporting. The business proved willingness to pay through $64 MRR in 2019, $2,750 MRR in July 2020 and $1M ARR in 2022.

The distribution stack rides on external surfaces: Hacker News, GitHub, Indie Hackers, Twitter, Reddit, Google Search and newsletter/community sharing. This is platform leverage, not evidence of illicit conduct.

Plausible explicitly markets open source, self-hosting and forkability as an escape from vendor lock-in. No customer-data hostage mechanism was found; the risk observed is competition/reselling of open code, answered by AGPLv3.

Early growth was explicitly reported without affiliate marketing or sponsorships, and the current About page says no affiliate or paid-endorsement spend. Six $5 donations were reported but were not a viable funding model.

No fundraising or customer prepayment pool was disclosed in the reviewed materials. The visible cash trigger was recurring subscription revenue; the source reports first salaries only after MRR had reached $5,035, but not owner draw or annual-prepay composition.

The retained pivot trail is product/business model evolution: first line of code, paid cloud, open-source MIT release, AGPLv3 defense, ClickHouse, salaries, Google Analytics import and Community Edition. A complete list of failed predecessor products was not found.

The owner-take-home proxy is $41,231–$46,301 before payroll, founder pay, tax, affiliate payouts, refunds and reinvestment, before payroll, tax, refunds, affiliate payouts, advertising, and reinvestment.

observations.text: The first 10–30 paying customers came after an underperforming Product Hunt launch and a next-day Hacker News launch that reached the top spot for about nine hours. The founder later identified Google Search and developer recommendations as durable channels.

The incumbent did not disappear; its self-inflicted weaknesses were the free-but-data-funded model, cookie/banner and privacy concerns, heavy/complex analytics, and GA4 migration/re-coding pain. Developers became internal salespeople for the alternative.

The purchase trigger is a company wanting privacy-friendly analytics, no cookie banner, simpler reporting and historical-data import despite Google Analytics being free. The founder explicitly identifies “free” as the main blocker to payment.

The business rides on Hacker News, Product Hunt, Google Search, boilerplate code, free personal projects and developer-to-company recommendations. The free plan is intentionally used as an ambassador/inside-sales loop.
The company advertises historical-data import from Google Analytics and easy API export, so the reviewed material shows an anti-lock-in posture. No customer-data hostage mechanism was found.
The affiliate mechanism is concrete: 50% of first-year revenue, with the promoter anonymized from the customer. The founder simultaneously says affiliate marketing was not a major growth driver.

The dashboard distinguishes MRR from immediate cash flow and annual subscriptions are normalized monthly, but the public materials do not disclose annual-prepay mix, refunds, taxes or customer cash timing.
